title: Bananas (per lb)

drivers.name: Price increase to $0.68 (+1.5%)
drivers.evidence: No lift observed at $0.68 in past weeks; baseline already incorporates seasonal and price noise. Noise-adjusted estimate for 1.5% price increase is -1.5% (shrunk toward 0).

adjustment.analysis: The baseline median of 438.2 is supported by strong historical trends and seasonal patterns. The price increase to $0.68 (+1.5%) is minor and recent weeks show no meaningful lift at this price. The 2026-09-28 week (470 units at $0.68) was close to baseline and no promotion occurred. The Labor Day dip (241 units) was event-driven and not price-related. No seasonal or promotional drivers are active in the target week. The classical uplift model finds no signal, and the noise-adjusted effect of price changes is negligible. No evidence of price sensitivity beyond baseline noise.

brief:
PRODUCT: Bananas (per lb) | category Produce | Store #12 (Austin, TX)
TARGET WEEK: 2026-11-09 to 2026-11-15 (5 weeks after the last week with sales data)

KNOWN PLAN FOR THE TARGET WEEK:
  events: none
  shelf price: 0.68 (+1.5% vs regular price 0.67)

STATISTICAL BASELINE (exponential smoothing of recent sales; it ignores events, promotions and prices):
  median 438.2 | 5%-95%: 312.6 - 556.1 | 10%-90%: 346.5 - 529.1

In the evidence below, 'vs baseline' = actual units / what this same baseline predicted for that week.
It is the multiplier that would have been right, so it maps directly onto median_multiplier.
This product's ordinary weeks already swing about +/-21% around the baseline, so a past effect smaller than that, seen only a few times, is mostly noise. The
'noise-adjusted estimate' is the effect shrunk toward x1.0 for that noise and the number of sightings.
